## Timeline of the Breach and Discovery
On or around **March 20, 2025**, Cargills Bank — a commercial bank in Sri Lanka — fell victim to a major cyberattack. A ransomware group known as **Hunters International** infiltrated the bank’s network, marking what appears to be the largest data breach in Sri Lankan history. The bank, which is publicly listed, had a legal obligation to disclose such incidents to the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE). It did so on March 21, but the initial disclosure vastly **downplayed the severity** — describing only an “unauthorized access to a peripheral system” with no impact on core operations. In reality, the attackers had **accessed a trove of sensitive data**.

Over the next few days, the situation escalated. By around **March 24–25**, the hackers began **dumping the stolen data online**, after what was likely a failed ransom negotiation. However, this admission came only after the data had already been posted on a dark web forum. For several days, the breach remained largely **out of the public eye** — with no immediate media coverage or public announcements by the bank beyond those terse stock exchange filings.

The breach truly came to light for the broader public at the end of March. On March 29, a social media alert by a local page (Numbers.lk) and ensuing discussions on Reddit and Twitter exposed the magnitude of the leak. An independent tech writer, Dinidu de Alwis, began examining the leaked files on March 30 after seeing these alerts. What he and others discovered shocked the Sri Lankan tech community: approximately **1.9 terabytes** of data (over **1.1 million files**) from Cargills Bank had been stolen and leaked.

## Nature and Scope of the Leaked Data
The **data leaked** in this incident was extensive and highly sensitive. It was not just a small subset of information, but appeared to be a comprehensive dump of customer and internal files.

## Who Is Behind the Attack?
The breach has been attributed to a professional hacker group — specifically a **ransomware gang** — calling itself **Hunters International**. This group is relatively new, emerging in late 2023, but it appears to be a **resurrection of the notorious Hive ransomware operation** that was disrupted by law enforcement in early 2023.

Hunters International operates as a **Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS)** outfit. In the Cargills Bank attack, they appear to have prioritized **data theft over encryption** of systems. The data was ultimately **posted on a dark web leak site** when the bank presumably refused or failed to meet ransom demands.

There is no indication this was an inside job. The **attack vector** is not yet confirmed publicly, but the leaked audit reports suggest multiple weaknesses — from unpatched systems to lax device controls — that could have been exploited.

The bank’s communications were noticeably **vague about the scope of the breach**. Nowhere did it quantify the leak (1.9TB) or list the types of data compromised. Behind the scenes, however, the Sri Lankan **government acknowledged** this may be the **largest data breach in the country’s history**.

## Conclusion
The Cargills Bank data leak is a **watershed moment** for Sri Lanka.
